nodes.title: Argument
nodes.normalizedStatement: An argument is a sequence of statements, the last of which is called the conclusion and the rest of which are called premises . An argument is said to be valid provided the conclusion must be true whenever the premises are all true. An argument is invalid if it is not valid; that is, all the premises can be true, and the conclusion could still be false. An argument is sound provided it is valid and all the premises are true. A proof of a statement is a sound argument whose conclusion is the statement.

nodes.title: Logical Connectives
nodes.normalizedStatement: We define the following logical connectives . P \wedge Q is read P and Q , and is called a conjunction . \wedge logical and (conjunction) P \vee Q is read P or Q , and is called a disjunction . \vee logical or (disjunction) P \imp Q is read if P then Q , and is called an implication or conditional . P \iff Q is read P if and only if Q , and is called a biconditional . \neg P is read not P , and is called a negation . \neg logical negation

nodes.title: Truth Conditions for Connectives
nodes.normalizedStatement: The truth conditions for the logical connectives are defined as follows. P \wedge Q is true when both P and Q are true. P \vee Q is true when P or Q or both are true. P \imp Q is true when P is false or Q is true (or both). P \iff Q is true when P and Q are both true, or both false. \neg P is true when P is false.

nodes.title: Implication
nodes.normalizedStatement: An implication (or conditional ) is a molecular statement of the form P \imp Q where P and Q are statements. We say that P is the hypothesis (or antecedent ). Q is the conclusion (or consequent ). An implication is true provided P is false or Q is true (or both), and false otherwise. In particular, the only way for P \imp Q to be false is for P to be true and Q to be false.

nodes.title: Necessary and Sufficient
nodes.normalizedStatement: P is necessary for Q means Q \imp P . P is sufficient for Q means P \imp Q . If P is necessary and sufficient for Q , then P \iff Q .

nodes.title: Logical Equivalence
nodes.normalizedStatement: Two (molecular) statements P and Q are logically equivalent provided P is true precisely when Q is true. That is, P and Q have the same truth value under any assignment of truth values to their atomic parts. We write this as P \equiv Q .

nodes.title: Theorem at sec_logic-rules.ptx:588
nodes.normalizedStatement: An implication is logically equivalent to its contrapositive. That is, P \imp Q \equiv \neg Q \imp \neg P .

nodes.title: Negation of an Implication
nodes.normalizedStatement: The negation of an implication is a conjunction: \neg(P \imp Q) \equiv P \wedge \neg Q . That is, the only way for an implication to be false is for the hypothesis to be true AND the conclusion to be false.

nodes.title: Mini Sudoku Definitions
nodes.normalizedStatement: A mini sudoku puzzle is a partially filled in 4\times 4 grid of squares, divided into four 2\times 2 boxes. Each square can be empty or contain a digit from 1 to 4. We say that a mini sudoku puzzle is valid provided no digit from 1 to 4 appears more than once in any row, any column, or any box. A solution to a mini sudoku puzzle is a valid puzzle with no empty squares and every non-empty square of the puzzle unchanged. We say that a mini sudoku puzzle is solvable if there is exactly one solution.

nodes.title: Definition at sec_logic-structures.ptx:303
nodes.normalizedStatement: A set A is a subset of a set B , written A \subseteq B , provided every element of A is also an element of B . The set B is sometimes called a superset of A . We say A is a proper subset of B , written A \subset B , provided A \subseteq B and A \neq B . In other words, if every element in A is an element in B , and there is at least one element in B that is not in A .

nodes.title: Definition at sec_gt-intro.ptx:691

Two graphs are isomorphic if there is an isomorphism between them. In this case we write G_1 \isom G_2 .

nodes.title: Trees and Forests
nodes.normalizedStatement: A tree is a connected graph containing no cycles. Sometimes this is stated as a tree is an acyclic connected graph; acyclic is just a fancy word for containing no cycles. A forest is a graph containing no cycles. Note that this means that a connected forest is a tree.

nodes.title: Reflexive, Symmetric, and Transitive
nodes.normalizedStatement: Let R be a relation on the set A . We say, R is reflexive provided (a,a) \in R for all a \in A . R is symmetric provided, for all a, b \in A , if (a,b) \in R then (b,a) \in R . R is transitive provided, for all a, b,c \in A , if (a,b) \in R and (b,c) \in R , then (a,c)\in R .

nodes.title: Equivalence Relation
nodes.normalizedStatement: A relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive is called an equivalence relation .

nodes.title: Definition at sec_gt-relations.ptx:814
nodes.normalizedStatement: Let R be a relation on the set A , and let a be an element of A . The relation class of a , written [a] is the set of all elements b such that (a,b) \in R (the set of b that are related to a by R ). That is, [a] = \{b \in A \st (a,b) \in R\} . When R is an equivalence relation, we call relation classes equivalence classes .

nodes.title: Definition at sec_gt-relations.ptx:888
nodes.normalizedStatement: Given a non-empty set A , a partition of A is a set P of non-empty subsets of A such that every element of A is in exactly one element of P .

nodes.title: Theorem at sec_gt-relations.ptx:949
nodes.normalizedStatement: Given any equivalence relation R on a set A , the equivalence classes form a partition of A . Given any partition P = \{B_1, B_2, \ldots, \} of a set A , the relation \equiv_P defined by a \equiv_P b if and only if a and b belong to the same block of P , is an equivalence relation. Further, the equivalence classes for the equivalence relation formed by a partition are exactly the original partition, and the equivalence relation built by the partition of its equivalence classes is exactly the original equivalence relation.

nodes.title: Binomial Theorem
nodes.normalizedStatement: The n th row of Pascal's triangle gives the coefficients of the expansion of (x+y)^n . That is, for any positive integer n , (x+y)^n = \binom{n}{0}x^n + \binom{n}{1}x^{n-1}y + \cdots + \binom{n}{n-1}xy^{n-1} + \binom{n}{n}y^n. , so the coefficient of x^ky^{n-k} is \binom{n}{k} .

nodes.title: Sum Principle
nodes.normalizedStatement: If an event A results in m outcomes, and event B results in n disjoint outcomes, then the event A or B results in m + n outcomes.

nodes.title: Product Principle

nodes.title: Sum Principle (with sets)
nodes.normalizedStatement: Given two sets A and B , if A \cap B = \emptyset , then \card{A \cup B} = \card{A} + \card{B} .

nodes.title: Cardinality of a Union (2 Sets)

nodes.title: Theorem at sec_counting-probability.ptx:577

nodes.title: Definition at sec_counting-probability.ptx:656
